sentences.text: Andy.
Andy.
To my friends.
Anyway.
All right.
Okay.
This meeting is being recorded.
I think we could be.
So who have I got?
The camera's not on.
Is that Wayne Ropelato and Shane Blakely?
Well, nice to meet you.
Thank you guys for your time today.
Whereabouts are you calling from?
Where are you based?
We're in Utah.
Ah, Utah.
Fantastic.
And where are you?
I'm in Somerset, in England.
So that's in the southwest of England.
But yeah, we work all the way across the US most of our.
Most of our work is actually US based.
Okay.
So we've only got 15 minutes.
So I can be as quick.
Quick as you like.
But I read through the.
The meeting notes that we had on the conversations that you've been having with Amanda and Jeff.
So it would be good to sort of get into it a little bit about what it is that you guys are looking to achieve.
I'll tell you a little bit about us.
We're capital A group and we are M and a advisory for marketing services companies.
And we work on both the buy and the sell side.
As you know, we were working with Skyview when we approach you.
So we work with sort of high growth companies, either their agencies already and they're looking to acquire more, or we work with private investors or private equity as well.
And then on the sell side, we have agencies co, which is our marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell their businesses.
So I'll be keen to know where you guys are at White Clouds and where you are in the.
The sort of decision process of selling your business.
And then I'll be happy to take you through our process as well quickly to explain what it is that we do and how we can help you.
So Andy, kind of, kind of where it was, is Amanda kind of cold?
Called us, what, a month, month and a half ago through Jeff out of New York.
We've actually never talked to him.
We kind of went through Amanda.
Oh, okay.
So it wasn't, you know, we.
We just kind of going through the grind of everyday work, work, work.
And she said that Jeff, through hovercraft.
We was familiar with hovercraft.
A couple years ago we did a partnership job with them.
Yeah, the NBA, Nike, all Stargate.
So anyway, she said they had an interest in looking at us.
We give them some information or I give Amanda information.
And I.
There must be something in the information that didn't strike Jeff as exciting or something because I haven't heard back from anything.
And then Amanda had reached out and said, hey, would you be interested in talking to our CEO about going forward with somebody else if it's a possibility.
So I said, yeah, you know, I. I don't like to ever say no to anything that's.
That's got a possibility or potential.
Yeah.
So I guess, to answer your question, we actively haven't been calling or trying to get people to buy into us or buy us.
Yeah.
So I don't know if that helps you kind of understand where we're at.
Yeah, of course.
I mean, that's.
That's helpful to.
To know that you're not actively looking.
But many times, you know, owners of businesses are looking at succession plans or.
Or just interested in what the next steps might be.
But it could be that your intentions are just to keep running white clouds until you are in the white clouds yourselves.
I. I don't know.
So.
I like that.
You know, Andy, let's be honest.
The right deal comes along, nobody's gonna say no.
Yeah, exactly.
And if.
And if the right deal comes along, but.
But it's good to kind of understand as well what it is that would be the right deal for you.
So just on.
On the.
The point about Jeff, it hasn't 100% shaken out just yet.
I think what happened was there was a bunch of leads that Amanda had that were just kind of paused until the fall because they were busy closing a deal that we'd set up for them.
So that deal closed last week, and now things are starting to move forward again everywhere else.
The thing is, we've obviously got some details from you already, but I guess I really just want to understand what it is that you guys would be looking for in terms.
This is nothing to do with Jeff.
It's just in terms of your own timeline, what you would be looking to do, if anything.
You know, that's a good question, Andy.
You know, internally in here, do we have an exit strategy that we're going down for an exit strategy?
We haven't really got down in the nuts and bolts of that, I can tell you.
The old.
The owner of our company is pushing 70 years old.
You know, I just don't see him wanting to be around for much longer, honestly.
You know, is there somebody in the company that if something happened to him today, would they take over?
Probably not much interest in that arena.
So I don't know if that helps you get an understanding, but, I mean, in my mind, I'm.
I'm president, and I'm turning 65 here in three more months.
I personally would like to see an exit strategy within two to three years or sooner.
Just depends if the right deal comes along, the one that Jeff has with Hovercraft in them, I think we're a perfect fit to throw something together, at least have some conversations in that arena.
We have a piece of the pie that they need and I think they have a piece of the pie that we could use.
And so, you know, just, I think there's a win win in there for both sides.
Okay.
And, and so who, who is the owner?
Is that, is that Jerry?
Jerry, yes.
And is, is Jerry sick or is he just lost interest in the company?
No, he still does day to day on it.
Oh, okay.
All right.
But, but there's, there's no exit plan, basically.

So if, if, if you could get something, I guess that was attractive up in, in front of Jerry, then that would be good for everybody because it would give more certainty about what would happen in, in the next three to five years.
Oh, absolutely, absolutely.
All right, so look just where you are.
So Your numbers are 6.2 million top line revenue.
I guess you spend quite a bit of that on producing the actual things that you make.
You know, we're a custom fab shop and so every project we do, some of them are two day jobs and some of them are six month jobs.
We usually on a day to day basis, we probably are working on close to 25 jobs at any given time.
We have about generally.
Well, our queue, our production queue usually runs anywhere between 80 and 120 jobs.
I, I can tell you this right now.
In our production queue we have, I think it's $1.1 million worth of work sitting there that's been unpaid for as of today.
Wow.
I like to be transparent, Andy, because I'm like, I, I know how these.
I, I work for another company for Jerry that they, we did an exit strategy.
It was top 10 reviews.
And I just know at some point in time guys are going to ask you for your financials and there's, it just doesn't do you any good not to be transparent right out of the gate.
Yeah, no, definitely.
And we've spoke to some production companies before, some fabrication shops that are heavily underwater.
So I know Jeff is definitely interested in speaking to more and would be interesting to talk to White Clouds, given that you've worked with Hovercraft.
But yeah, I mean there is always a worry around, around the financials and whether a business is solid and can survive being acquired.

But are you saying that that 1.1 million that's in production hasn't been paid for are you struggling to make sure that you're able to get that revenue in or is that just a normal part of the process?
That's kind of what we run around the clock.
Day to day is basically about a million dollars.
Okay.
So you usually would collect that, but it's, it's got like 30 to 90 days on it.
Yeah, it's a backlog of work.
We know that we run best and we've got backlog.
We don't ever want to run day to day.
Okay.
So you could, you could do more if the, if the company had the investment.
You mean with more people?
We, we do have options for running a second shift or adding to our current staff.
Right.
Okay.
Or.
Jeff.
Sorry, Andy.
One, one problem we have here in Utah.
Real estate right now as far as buildings.
It's pretty tight and has been since COVID There hasn't been a lot of growth with people building buildings.
But we actually, let's see, we're probably, we probably are.
We have three buildings right now and we probably cover about 30,000 square feet.
We are actively looking for a building right now that takes us to 60 to 70,000 square feet.
And we know for a fact that we could fill that with employees and work easily.
It's just basically we, we are at max capacity now.
Any investors say, well, why aren't you running a swing and a graveyard shift to keep it going?
I think we feel the pains of everybody in the country.
Right.
Maybe everybody in the world right now.
It's hard to get people to want to go do physical, hands on manual work.
Everybody wants to work in the basement from home.
Yeah, fair enough.
Hard skip manual workers.
Well, so do you have sort of limited people, new people that are joining the company that you're able to train into the business?
We basically are hiring.
We're hiring and interviewing at all times.
We just, if the right person comes along, we offer them a job and get them in here.
Okay.
But we're not.
I.
The days of just hiring a human, a human body just to be a body, a warm body, I'm done with that.
That doesn't get you anywhere.
Okay.
Okay.
So.
All right, that's, that's interesting.
Yeah.

So, so look, just, just because I'm about to, to talk to Jeff in about an hour just on the company, then you guys are, are still keen to, to speak with Jeff and you think Jerry would be, be interested in selling just on the valuation?
I don't know what Jeff would offer to you, but, but around 500k EBITDA is, is something like a 4x multiple.
Do you know what Jerry is looking for to exit?
Has he, has he ever discussed numbers or do you guys have like an internal thing that, that you would sort of suggest?
I, you know, just kind of me and him and I'm going back about two years ago.
He, I, I think he was looking to be in that 10 to 15 million range at some point to get out.
10 to 15 million.
And is there, is there property involved in the business that would push the valuation up?
That real estate property?
No, but equipment, right?
Yes.
So I don't know how you, how you would divvy that up.
So the equipment is the, the expensive stuff?
Yeah, CNC machines.
We got a couple.
Okay, well, yeah, we would have to take a look at that and see, see what that was.
I mean that is always the difficulty is invest equipment because you're constantly having to reinvest, aren't you?
After a certain number of years you've got to keep buying more, better equipment.
And Andy, I don't, I don't know the value of this to how it would play out.
I just know about two years ago I was in a meeting one day with Jerry and he threw out if somebody ever bought this company, there's a 10 million tax write off.
That's a carryover or a rollover from him putting in the initial investment.
Right.
I think this is probably more in your arena than mine.
I'm just sharing with you what, what I know.
It's, it's good, it's good to know.
Okay, so he's in, he's invested in equipment maybe to the value of, of around 10 million.
So that's what he would be able to, to write off against any profits somewhere else in the business.
Okay, that, that's also interesting to know.
Okay, look, like I said, I'm, I'm speaking to, to Jeff.
I guess he would be interested in, in seeing if there's a way that you guys could, could work together given that you've been working via hovercraft already.

Do you have like, I know you've got a, a great website with a, a bunch of your work on the front page, but do you have any sort of up to date marketing materials that, that kind of shows your capabilities?
You have like a deck or anything that you normally share.
I could get you one that'd be.
Really, really handy if I, if I could get hold of something like that and I could talk it through with Jeff then and see, you know, whether that, that aligns with their requirements.
Going forward, because if.

If it was something, you know, if you're producing the sort of work that hovercraft they're already paying for externally, if they could bring that in in house, then that obviously makes a lot of sense.
Yes.
Yeah.
So it'd be good to have that.
Okay, how about I ping you an email after this, then, just so you can fire it back at me?
Like I said, I'm speaking to Jeff in about an hour and 10 minutes.
Let me see what you come up with.
Yeah, that'd be fantastic.
And I'll.
I'll talk to him about the situation with.
With Jerry and yourself.
Are you guys related?
Are you brothers or.
Yeah, we're brothers.
Okay.
All right, fantastic.
Look, good to.
Good to meet you both.
Thank you for your time.

And I. I'm hoping that we're going to have more discussions that are a bit more in depth as well, but I. I just need to get up to date with where Jeff is on the fabrication side of things, so I'll ask him explicitly.
All right, have a great day, guys.
I really appreciate your time.
All right, speak soon.

summary.action_items:
**Wayne Ropelato / Shane Blakely**
Provide Andy Day with up-to-date marketing materials/deck to support conversation with Jeff regarding strategic fit and possible deal (15:45)

**Andy Day**
Follow up with Jeff regarding White Clouds’ situation, valuation expectations, and explore interest in pursuing acquisition or strategic partnership (15:44)
Send follow-up email to White Clouds initiating request for marketing materials and preparing Jeff discussion agenda (15:45)
summary.overview:
- Wayne Ropelato and Shane Blakely opened the meeting with Andy Day, discussing potential synergies and strategies in M&A advisory, highlighting their expertise in marketing services.
- White Clouds, reached through Amanda, is passively evaluating opportunities despite not seeking buyers actively, indicating tentative openness for discussions.
- Company owner Jerry, nearing 70, lacks a succession plan; Wayne aims for an exit strategy in 2-3 years, showing flexibility in the timeline.
- White Clouds reported approximately $6.2 million in top-line revenue, with a $1.1 million backlog, signifying a strong production pipeline.
- The company is managing about 25 concurrent jobs while maintaining a production queue of 80-120 jobs, reflecting robust operational capacity.
- White Clouds plans to double their facilities from 30,000 sq ft to 60,000-70,000 sq ft, indicating intentions for scaling operations.
- Nationwide labor shortages are hindering hiring for manual production roles, emphasizing a strategy of prioritizing quality over quantity in recruitment.
- Jerry's informal exit valuation target was $10 to $15 million two years ago, necessitating strategic consideration of company equipment in the overall valuation.
- A potential $10 million tax write-off related to capital investment was noted, adding complexity and tax advantages to the acquisition process.
- Next steps include Andy Day discussing strategic fit with Jeff and requesting updated marketing materials from White Clouds for further consideration.
summary.short_summary: During the meeting, President Wayne Blakely discussed White Clouds' openness to an exit opportunity within the next two to three years, influenced by his age and owner Jerry's nearing 70. Jerry remains involved but lacks interest in long-term succession, with no internal successor identified. Financially, the company generates $6.2 million in annual revenue but faces a $1.1 million backlog and capacity limitations due to space and labor shortages. Hiring skilled labor remains a challenge, impacting production despite demand. Valuation expectations are high, with Jerry seeking $10 to $15 million, influenced by equipment investments and tax considerations. The meeting also explored potential synergies with Hovercraft, given their past collaborations and complementary capabilities, with plans for further discussions on deal terms.
